`docs/security.md` reddens the census test with "names an unshipped directory", which is the CI failure
reproduced locally rather than discovered remotely; restoring returns it to green with the file re-hashed in the
same command. The control test asserts both fakes are reported -- a made-up module and a made-up path under
`build/` -- so the second rule cannot be silently dropped.

The shape to keep: a check that reads the filesystem is only as portable as the filesystem it reads. Existence
was the wrong predicate; "a reader can open this from a clone" is the right one, and that is a statement about
what is shipped, not about what is present.

## 271. "MIME sniff" named a module nothing calls, and the number I wrote for it came from a truncated read

`docs/api.md` advertised the upload as `multipart, 100MB, MIME sniff, archive bomb guard`, and `docs/security.md`
listed `packages/execution/src/dsa_execution/mime_sniff.py` as a file gatekeeper beside `validate.py`. Measured:
`dsa_execution.mime_sniff` -- the module with the magic-byte `sniff_mime`, the `is_allowed_mime` decision and
`looks_like_zip_bomb` -- has **no production caller**. Its only consumer is `tests/unit/test_coverage_sweep.py`,
which asserts its behaviour and thereby makes it look enforced. What actually runs on `POST /api/v1/datasets/` is
a table duplicated inside `validate_file`, whose own comment says it was copied from `mime_sniff` to avoid an
import cycle, and that table checks the **client-declared** content type. Declared-type filtering is a legitimate
control; it is not sniffing, and the two documents said it was.

The divergence between the two rules was measured over 66 (extension, declared type, body) combinations: 29
agree, 0 cases where the live rule accepts what the sniffer refuses, and 37 the other way -- so the shipped rule
is strictly stricter. The mechanism is the sniffer's fallback: an unrecognized declaration is replaced by
`sniff_mime`, which answers from the extension's own guessed type, so `.xls` declared `text/csv` passes because
csv is allowed for xls. Every allowed extension diverges, which is why wiring the sniffer in later would loosen
the gate rather than tighten it, and why the finding was written as a direction and a mechanism rather than a
pattern-match list.

Then my own number was wrong, and the correction is the point of this section. The first probe printed
`disagreements: N` on a line that `tail -14` cut off, and the rows I could see named only `.xlsx`/`.xls`, so I
wrote "they agree on 52 and the sniffer additionally accepts 14" into `docs/security.md`. Both figures were
wrong -- 29 and 37 -- and the scope claim ("only the Excel pair") was wrong too. It was caught only because the
test written afterwards asserted the count and the extension set rather than restating the prose: the run
answered 37 and named all six extensions. A digit read through a truncating pipe is a transcription, and this
is the second time this month that a guard computed from the artifact caught what an eye had accepted.

`docs/api.md` now says the upload's type rule is a client-declared allowlist; `docs/security.md` names
`validate.py` as the single owner, states that the sniffer is not wired, and says wiring it would loosen the
gate. Two new tests in `tests/security/test_upload_guard.py` hold that: the differential, with the direction and
the count pinned, and an AST scan asserting no shipped module imports `mime_sniff` -- AST because `validate.py`
contains the string `mime_sniff` in the very comment that explains why it does not import it, and a text scan
would report that comment as a caller. The first is falsified by tightening the sniffer's `.xls` entry to an
empty set, which makes the live rule the looser one and reddens it naming that case; the second by planting a
temporary module that imports it, then removing it and proving it is gone.

## 272. The sandbox's wall-clock timeout bounds reported time, not occupied time -- measured at both ends

`docs/security.md` listed "wall-clock timeout" among the Python guard's controls. `_LoopDeadline` documents its
own coverage honestly -- pure-Python iteration is interruptible at loop heads, "a single long call into C still
runs to completion and is only reported afterwards" -- so the check was not whether the code lies, but whether
the sentence around it carries the caveat. Measured on 2026-10-23 with `timeout_ms=300`:

- `while True: n += 1` -- wall clock 0.33 s, reported 312 ms, `TimeoutError`. The deadline fires, within one
  frame of the budget.
- `np.matmul(np.ones((3200, 3200)), np.ones((3200, 3200)))` -- wall clock 0.34 s, reported 331 ms,
  `TimeoutError`. The matrix multiply ran to its natural end; the budget was noticed afterwards. Same code at a
  1000 ms budget: 0.37 s, no error, which is the control that says the first answer was not just a slow machine.

So the timeout is a *reporting* bound for C calls and only an *execution* bound for interpreted loops. That is
worth one sentence in a security document because the two behave differently under the only threat that matters
here: an anonymous caller who can reach `/mcp` can occupy an API worker for as long as one call takes, and on a
0.5-vCPU free instance the cheapest way to make the demo slow is not exfiltration but arithmetic. No plant was
run that deliberately outlasted tens of seconds -- the 331 ms case is enough to show the mechanism, and the
matmul size is a knob a reader can turn in their own head rather than on their own CPU.

The doc line now says which half is enforced, cites the module's own docstring, and names the availability
consequence next to #59. The loop case and the C-call case are both in the sentence because a claim about a
mechanism needs both directions, and the second one is what stops the reader assuming the budget is a wall.

## 273. One of my own commits describes the wrong diff

`59e356a` contains `HANDOFF-2026-10-19.md` and nothing else -- a twenty-eighth addendum and one witness line --
and its message describes the *previous two* commits instead: the sandbox timeout measurement and the
"declared type, when present" fix. The content is the right content in the right place; the subject line is a
record of work that lives under other SHAs.

Why this belongs in the ledger rather than quietly: `git show <sha>` is the instrument a future reader uses to
answer "what did this commit change", and after this one the honest answer is "not what the message says".
Amending is not an option -- the commit is pushed, and rewriting a published commit is the class of action that
this repository's rules reserve for the owner. So the correction is a sentence here plus the habit it argues
for: a commit whose diff is only the handoff log says so in its subject, because the log's own message is the
one place where "what I meant" and "what changed" have to agree.

Nothing about the product's behaviour moved in `59e356a`, so no doc, test, or CHANGELOG entry needs to change:
the timeout claim (`docs/security.md`), the availability consequence, and the absent-declaration rule were all
shipped in `d9bafe7` and `48885f2` under their own accurate messages, and CI for those three heads is recorded
above. This is instrument hygiene, kept where instrument errors are kept.

The subject repeated before it was caught. `229f408` -- whose diff is this section alone -- carries the same
wrong line as `59e356a`, because the message was written from the round's narrative rather than from `git show
--stat` for the paths actually staged. Two adjacent commits now read as copies of each other. No force-push and
no amend: both are published, and rewriting published history is the owner's call, not a convenience for the
author. What was done instead is the thing a reader can use -- `HANDOFF-2026-10-19.md`'s twenty-eighth addendum
now carries a per-SHA inventory generated from `git show --name-only`, so the four SHAs of the round are matched
to their real file lists, and the two mislabelled ones are named as such. The habit that follows is mechanical:
read the stat for the paths being committed *before* writing the subject, every time, including for a commit
whose only content is a log entry.

## 274. The upload filename rule refuses `data..v2.csv` and accuses it of path traversal

`validate_filename` blocks the pattern `(\.\.|//|\\)` and separately rejects any `/` or `\`. The consequence,
measured 2026-10-23 without writing anything: `../evil.csv`, `a/../../etc/passwd` and `..\evil.csv` are refused
-- correctly -- and so are `data..v2.csv` and any other legitimate name whose middle happens to contain two
dots, with the message "Path traversal detected in filename". That message is false for the second group, and
the refusal is doing no work: the separator rule already ran, and the stored name is composed as
`f"{dataset_id}_{filename}"` (`apps/api/src/dsa_api/services/dataset_service.py:90`), so the uuid sits in front
and a leading `..` could not traverse even if the separator rule were gone. The claim in `docs/security.md`
-- "`..` traversal block" -- is true; what is not true is that the block is what stopped this filename.

Two ways to fix it, and they are not the same change. Narrow the rule to what traversal means -- refuse exactly
`.` and `..`, keep the separator refusal, accept interior double dots -- which turns a 400 into a 201 for
visitors uploading files named `Q1..Q2.csv`; or leave the rule and correct only the accusation, so the message
says the name may not contain a double dot rather than alleging traversal. The first is a behaviour change on
the upload endpoint and therefore the owner's call, so it is on the open list rather than done here; the second
is a string. Recorded before either, because a validation rule that fires on ordinary input and reports a
security reason for it trains everyone who sees it to distrust the security reason.

The existing tests are honest about the current behaviour and would move with either fix:
`tests/unit/test_datasets.py:23` covers `../etc/passwd` and `a/b.csv`, and neither case is the one this section
is about -- which is how a false positive survives a green traversal test.

## 275. Four pushes in four minutes cancelled three secret scans, and a cancelled scan is coverage that never happened

`.github/workflows/secret-scan.yml` runs gitleaks on every push to `main` under
`concurrency: secret-scan-push-main` with `cancel-in-progress: true`. That is the right shape for a check that
should not pile up on a busy branch, and it has a consequence nobody wrote down: when pushes land seconds
apart, the earlier runs are cancelled mid-scan, and because each run scans only its own push payload -- the
range `commits[0]..commits[-1]` of that event -- a cancelled range is not picked up by the next run. Four
pushes in the last few minutes left `59e356a`, `229f408` and `e553a64` with no completed secret scan, and the
tip `b0a592a` shows `completed / cancelled` as well. No peer pushed in between, so the cancels were my own
cadence cancelling each other.

The coverage question is then specific rather than rhetorical: were those commits scanned by anything? Their
content is prose -- ledger sections, the handoff addendum, doc sentences -- so the same shapes were checked
locally instead, with eight gitleaks-style patterns (AWS access key id, the five `gh*_` token families,
`github_pat_`, Slack app/user tokens, OpenAI-style `sk-`, a `Bearer <long>` value, a PEM private-key header,
and a generic `api_key|secret|passwd|password|token = "<12+>"` assignment) over every file this round touched:
zero hits. That is a substitute, not an equivalent -- gitleaks has more rules and its own entropy analysis --
so the honest entry is: those ranges are unscanned by CI, the local check found nothing secret-shaped in prose
only, and the durable fix is a scheduled full-history scan so that a cancel cannot silently reduce coverage.
That is a `.github/workflows` change, which is the owner's line to cross, so it is on the open list (#5, below
the other four) rather than done here.

Worth naming the general shape next to the existing note that "green does not mean the repo is clean": green
does not mean the range ran either, and `skipped`/`cancelled` on a check that is not a required status is
invisible to a reader looking only at the commit badge. The per-step read the handoff now does for CI is the
same read this finding asks for on the scan workflows.

§274 follow-up, same day -- the message was fixed and the policy was not.

`validate_filename` now refuses with the rule that fired: `'..'` reports `Filename must not contain '..' (path
traversal)`, a single separator reports `Filename must not contain path separators`. The `_UNSAFE_PATTERNS`
regex that mixed both -- `..`, `//` and `\` under one traversal sentence -- is gone, and the vendored twin was
re-synced and compared byte-for-byte.

The accept/reject set did not move, and that is asserted rather than argued: fifteen names were run through both
the old and the new predicate and the verdicts came out identical for all fifteen. The table now lives in
`tests/security/test_upload_guard.py` written out as literals rather than recomputed from the old rule, so a
future shift in one verdict shows up as a diff instead of a self-agreeing test. The first draft of that
table was written from the probe I remembered rather than the probe I ran, and got `.` wrong -- it landed
as `False`, the suite went red on `DID NOT RAISE`, and the fix was to re-run both predicates and paste
the verdicts. A behaviour-preservation table that is itself a transcription is worth nothing; this one is
now a measurement with the mistake in its history. One row is in it precisely
because it looks wrong at first glance: `validate_filename(".")` passes. It is stopped one line later by
`detect_format`, which finds no allowed extension -- and the test asserts that pair, because "which rule
actually refused this upload" is the same distinction the message fix is about.

Why the wording moved and not the neighbour's assertion: `tests/security/test_adversarial_suite.py:53` matches
the message against `traversal|separator|path`. Tightening their regex to my new strings would have worked and
was the wrong trade, editing someone else's contract to fit mine; keeping the reason in parentheses leaves
theirs passing, keeps the traversal vocabulary greppable in logs, and still stops accusing an ordinary
filename. Where both needs fit was the message; the regex was where they collided.

What is still the owner's call is the half this change did not take: refusing a name for containing two dots is
a policy, and narrowing it to `.`/`..` as whole segments would turn a 400 into a 201 for a visitor uploading
`Q1..Q2.csv`. Open item #71 carries that, and the refusal fires today exactly as it did before.
## 276. The dependency queue had three causes, and my own waiter invented a fourth
The queue looked like one job -- land the open Dependabot bumps -- and turned out to be three different
failures wearing the same clothes, plus one I built myself.

**Cause one was structural.** This repository keeps three npm lockfiles (root, `apps/web`, `apps/vscode`), so
every npm bump arrives as two half-PRs: one updating the member lock, one updating the root lock. Neither can
pass alone, because `npm --prefix apps/web ci` reads the member lock while
`scripts/check_npm_workspace_lock.py` compares the root lock against the member manifests. #87 and #88 were
closed as superseded rather than fixed -- measured first: `origin/main` already carried every version they
proposed (`react 19.3.1`, `react-dom 19.3.1`, `@types/react 19.3.0`, `react-is ^19.3.1`), so landing them would
have re-broken a passing state.

**Cause two was a member lock that cannot be regenerated where it lives.** `npm install` run inside
`apps/vscode` walks up to the workspace root: it reported `up to date in 372ms` and rewrote the ROOT lock,
leaving `apps/vscode/package-lock.json` untouched. The member lock has to be generated from a standalone copy of
the manifest in a directory with no parent workspace. #106 landed `@vscode/test-electron` 2.5.2 -> 3.1.0 that
way, with all three locks in step; the bump raises an engine floor from `node >= 16` to `>= 22`, which CI's Node
26 clears. The same measurement says something about that package: nothing imports it, `apps/vscode/src` is
`extension.ts`, `dsa.ts`, `views.ts`, and its `"test": "node ./out/test/suite.test.js"` names a source file that
does not exist -- so the guard that would catch a real 3.x break there is `tsc`, not a test runner.

**Cause three was mine.** My merge loop watched CI with `gh run watch --exit-status >/dev/null 2>&1` and read
any non-zero as "the run was not green". It is not: a watch can fail for its own reasons while the run is still
in progress. That false negative stopped the queue at #90, whose CI had finished `conclusion=success`. The
verdict now comes from the run's own `status`/`conclusion` fields, a `gh` error is printed as an error and
retried rather than becoming a finding, and only `completed` + non-success is a red. Falsified rather than
asserted: pointed at #91, which really is failing, the same function returns `RED:failure` -- which is what makes
its `GREEN` mean something. Two more instrument faults surfaced in the same hour, both of the "silence read as
evidence" kind: `set -- $line` does not word-split in zsh, so every PR came back as `PENDING:` with an empty
status -- not a wrong verdict but a wait that can never end -- and a `gh` call with no timeout stalled a poller
between `PENDING:in_progress` at 09:39 and its next line at 12:35. `echo "x_rc=$?"` after a pipeline reports
`sed`'s status, not the merge's, and `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` is bash-only: under zsh it prints `x_rc=?`.

**Dependabot cannot rebase what a human has touched.** #92 and #89 are `CONFLICTING`, and `@dependabot rebase`
answered "Looks like this PR has been edited by someone other than Dependabot." Both conflicts are in derived
files only (`uv.lock` and the two `release/sbom*`), so #109 re-derives each PR's own resolution on current main.
One piece of discipline there earned its keep: plain `uv lock --upgrade-package langchain-core==1.6.12` also
moved langsmith to 0.14.12, one patch past what #89 proposed and was green on, so langsmith is pinned back to
0.14.11 -- the goal is landing the reviewed change, not whatever is newest today.

**The SBOM still needs two steps, not one.** `generate_sbom.py` takes its component set from `uv.lock` but reads
every license from `importlib.metadata` of the *installed* environment. Run straight over the tracked files in a
fresh worktree it copies license strings off the pre-bump versions and writes `Unknown` for the four packages
nothing has installed -- and `--check` cannot see any of it, because it compares `(package, version)` pairs and
release version, and license is not one of the fields it reads. So: set from a `--out` scratch run, licenses
carried verbatim from HEAD for unchanged rows, the seven changed rows named from pypi.org. Asserted after: 0 rows
erased to `Unknown`, 0 unchanged rows whose license differs from HEAD.

**Ruff 0.17.1 was the risky half, because the bump replaces the gate itself**, so it was A/B'd on one tree:
`uvx ruff@0.16.3 check .` and `uvx ruff@0.17.1 check .` both print `All checks passed!`, and
`uvx ruff@0.17.1 format --check .` reports `315 files already formatted`. No new rule fires and no reformat is
owed.

**lucide 1.x deleted the brand icons, and the changelog was not the evidence.** Measured on the installed
package: `Github`, `Gitlab`, `Twitter`, `Facebook`, `Linkedin`, `Youtube` are all absent from 1.61.0's 6506 export
names, so #72 could not land as written -- the import at `apps/web/app/page.tsx:2` had to go. The mark is inlined
rather than traded for a second icon dependency; its two `d` strings are byte-for-byte those in
`lucide-react@0.545.0/dist/esm/icons/github.js`, checked against the 0.545 tree still on disk rather than against
memory. Asserted in a browser, not by reading JSX: 16x16 box, `viewBox 0 0 24 24`, `aria-hidden`, `fill none`, 2px
round/round stroke, and both paths with non-zero bounding boxes (`[4,2,16,20]`, `[2,16,7,2.6]`), identical at 1280
and 390 and in both locales. #105.

**Building the tour for another port was impossible, and the tour said so while telling you to do it.**
`assertBundleMatchesThisTree` refused any bundle origin whose port differed from `--api-port` -- but `lib/api.ts`
compiles `(configuredApiUrl || "http://localhost:8000")` and minification keeps the fallback, so a `:8010` build
always carries `:8000` too, and `--api-port 8010` exited 1 with an instruction to perform the build that had just
been done. CI never sees this: it always uses 8000, where the guarded port and the fallback are the same string.
The rule is now two-sided -- the port must be *present*, and nothing else may appear unless the source names it --
with the second half existing precisely so the first cannot be relaxed into a no-op for a bundle carrying no
loopback origin at all. Verified on one real tree in four configurations, then falsified by re-planting the old
one-sided rule: 3 of the 8 new tests go red. Writing that pin caught an asymmetry in my own fix -- presence
accepted `https://localhost:PORT` while the allow-list carried only the two `http` spellings, so a TLS loopback
build satisfied one edge and was refused by the other. #108.

**I also opened a duplicate and closed it.** `docs/FRONTEND_IA.md:269` cited
`build/r13f-nav-acceptance.mjs`, and `.gitignore:14` ignores `build/`, so that path exists only on the machine
that ran the original check. Reproduced both ways: `git archive origin/main | tar -x` +
`pytest tests/contract/test_doc_code_paths.py` exits 1 with
`assert not ['docs/FRONTEND_IA.md: `build/r13f-nav-acceptance.mjs`']`, while the same run in a working tree that
happens to hold the ignored script exits 0 -- which is why the commit that fixed twelve other dangling citations
left this one: green here, red there. I repointed the sentence (#110); `cd7a3a8` landed at 14:57:24, one minute
after my push, and did it better by moving the instrument to a tracked path and repairing its absolute playwright
import so the cited file can actually run for a reader. #110 is closed as superseded. Two lessons kept: re-measure
`origin/main` immediately before opening anything, and a guard that resolves citations with `.exists()` rather
than `git ls-files` will stay blind to any untracked file outside its named scratch directories -- stated on that
PR for whoever owns the guard, not fixed by me because the file is actively owned.

**Two things I did not do.** #91 and #102 fail `dependency-review`, and extending a gate's allowlist is not mine
to decide. The framing matters and is measured: `certifi@2026.10.19` reports `MPL-2.0` and `pillow@13.0.0` reports
`MIT-CMU`, neither in the allowed list -- but main already ships `certifi 2026.7.22` and `pillow 12.3.0`, and PyPI
reports the *same* identifiers for those current versions. `dependency-review` only inspects the lines a PR
changes, so any bump surfaces a pre-existing state as a fresh violation; the matplotlib `LicenseRef-scancode-*`
label is a separate question and should not be bundled with it. And
`check_public_claims.released_versions()` reads `<root>/.git/packed-refs` and `<root>/.git/refs/tags`, which do
not exist in a linked worktree where `.git` is a pointer file -- the same interpreter returns 38 tag entries in
the shared working tree and 0 in a worktree, which is what made two suite failures and the claims gate red locally
and has nothing to do with the dependency change. Fixing it needs care because `scripts/` is under bandit's S
rules and cannot shell out to git, so it is recorded rather than folded into a dependency PR.

## 277. One decision taken: the HTTP MCP surface no longer offers the tools that could run code

Owner chose the first option on 2026-10-23, the one that needed no new dependency, no new service and no
credential -- withhold rather than authenticate. `run_python` and `run_sql` are gone from every HTTP boundary of
the MCP app: `GET /mcp/tools`, `GET /tools`, `POST /mcp` `tools/list`, and both call shapes refuse them before
the dispatcher is reached. `dsa mcp` over stdio still publishes all 19, because that process is launched by the
person who owns the machine it runs on and its threat model never was a stranger on the network.

The refusal is `-32000`, in the block the JSON-RPC spec reserves for the server, not `-32601`: the tool exists,
this transport declines to run it, and a client that sees "unknown tool" has no way to learn the alternative.
The message names the tool and the way back (`run \`dsa mcp\` (stdio) to use it`), because a security refusal
that does not say what to do instead is indistinguishable from a broken deployment.

Three things in the implementation are deliberate:

- The excluded set is one `frozenset` in `dsa_mcp.adapter` and the filtered list is one function,
  `http_tools_for_wire()`. The `inputSchema` bug this module also fixed (§250) was five boundaries each
  serializing the same object their own way; a transport-level exclusion added at one of them would have had the
  same shape. `tests/security/test_mcp_http_surface.py` checks both HTTP routes plus the stdio control, and its
  refusals are witnessed by a trap that raises if `call_mcp_tool` is entered -- a check on the response body
  alone would pass on a refusal that ran the tool and then threw the result away.
- `profile_dataset` is left in place, and the docs say so out loud: the read and the path-existence oracle are
  unchanged, so this is a narrower surface and not a closed one. #59 stays open for the authentication half.
- Six existing tests encoded the old contract and were moved with it, not deleted: the conformance suite's
  "valid call" and "stateless repeat" now use a retained tool, its count assertion became a relation
  (`registry − withheld`) rather than a restated 19, `test_mcp_app_acceptance` likewise, and the resources-seam
  import guard now requires `http_tools_for_wire` instead of a `list_mcp_tools` the server no longer calls.
  That last one matters: leaving the import to satisfy the guard would have re-created the dead-code shape §271
  just spent a round documenting.

Measured after the change: five tool names fewer on HTTP, 17 published, and the App page unaffected because it
calls `profile_dataset` and `analyze` -- neither withheld.

## 278. The nightly sweep, and why a scan that can be cancelled is not a gate

`Secret Scan` answered the question "did this content get scanned" with "sometimes", and the reason is two
settings that are each individually reasonable: a push run takes its range from its own event payload, and
`cancel-in-progress: true` lets a newer push interrupt an older run. Four pushes in four minutes on
2026-10-23 therefore cancelled three scans whose ranges were never covered by anything else.

Fixed by the second half of the same owner decision: a `schedule` trigger at 04:37 daily, where no event range
exists so gitleaks walks the whole history `fetch-depth: 0` checked out, and
`cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name != 'schedule' }}` -- push and PR runs keep their fast-feedback
cancellation, the backstop cannot be interrupted. The first step of every run now prints its own `SCOPE=`, so
the log answers the coverage question instead of leaving the reader to infer it from a green tick, which is the
same "read the step, not the badge" discipline the CI jobs are run under.

`tests/security/test_w7_supply_chain.py::test_secret_scan_workflow` went from `"gitleaks" in txt.lower()` to
six named properties -- schedule present, parseable cron, the non-cancellable sweep, `fetch-depth: 0`, the
pinned `GITLEAKS_VERSION`, and the `SCOPE=` line. Falsified against the previous file: restored the old
workflow, the test reddens; put the new one back, green. A guard that would also pass on the broken state is the
thing this repository keeps having to discover.

## 279. The licence half of the queue was never a dependency problem, and clearing it grew a different risk class

§276 left #91 and #102 to the owner because extending a licence allowlist is a policy call. That call has now
been made and landed (#120), and the interesting part is not the versions -- it is that the gate was red for a
reason the gate itself cannot see, and that clearing the queue immediately produced work of a different kind.

**The blocker was an artefact of what `dependency-review` inspects.** The action looks only at lock lines a PR
*changes*. A dependency that already ships is never asked about, so the first bump to touch it reports a
pre-existing state as if it were newly introduced. Measured against main before the change:
`release/sbom.json` already recorded `certifi@2026.7.22` with license `MPL-2.0` -- the project's own published
SBOM had been asserting that licence for weeks -- and `matplotlib@3.11.1` already stored the free text
"License agreement for matplotlib versions 1.3.0 and later", which is what scancode turns into
`LicenseRef-scancode-matplotlib-1.3.0`. PyPI reports the same `license_expression` for pillow 12.3.0 as for
13.0.0. So all three identifiers describe licences already shipped; the PRs surfaced them, they did not add
them. That distinction is the whole reason `allow-licenses` grew from seven names to ten while
`fail-on-severity: high` and `fail-on-scopes: runtime` were left exactly alone -- widening which names count as
known is not the same change as weakening what is checked.

**The policy change is its own commit.** `0738d5c` carries the four bumps and the SBOM; `a5f7e28` carries the
allowlist and nothing else. Bundling them would have made the licence decision revertible only by unpicking
dependency versions, and it would have removed the independent witness: with both in one commit, the gate goes
green for a reason a reader cannot separate from the bump itself.

**One claim in that PR was explicitly not verifiable locally, and CI settled it.** `allow-licenses` matching is
exact, and the scancode label came from the action's own failure text rather than from a registry of permitted
names. Stated as an open risk before merging, with the commitment that a wrong spelling would be corrected or
reported -- not quietly deleted to force the check green. CI's `dependency-review` then passed with the label
verbatim. `dependency-review` is not a required context here (branch protection requires only `ci`), so the
guess was cheap to make and cheap to be wrong about; that is why it was allowed to be a guess at all.

**pillow 12 -> 13 was the only real risk in the change**, being matplotlib's runtime image dependency and a major
version. It was installed and exercised rather than argued with: `uv sync --frozen` confirming all four versions,
then `uv run pytest -q --cov` at 84.21% coverage against the 79% floor with exactly two failures --
`test_currency_claims.py` and `test_announcement_currency.py`, both asserting "no tags readable from this
checkout", the linked-worktree `.git`-pointer condition from §276 again. Control in a tree whose `.git` is a
directory: those two files pass, 29 tests. The SBOM rebuild kept the same discipline as the previous bump:
assert zero rows erased to `Unknown` and zero unchanged rows whose licence moved *before* writing, and `Unknown`
went 133 -> 131 because pillow and langgraph-sdk now carry real identifiers.

**Then the queue refilled, with different risk.** Eight new Dependabot PRs appeared within the hour (#112-#119),
and four of them are not maintenance: `typescript 5.9.3 -> 7.0.2`, `tailwind-merge 2.6.1 -> 3.7.0`,
`@types/node 20.19.43 -> 26.6.5`, `statsmodels 0.14.6 -> 0.15.0`. They were left open deliberately. A toolchain
major version is a migration with its own blast radius -- Tailwind 3 -> 4 in this same round was its own PR
(#103, `fix(web): Tailwind 3 -> 4, removing the last reason the npm advisory list existed`, recorded at
`CHANGELOG.md:799`), and it still reads in the tree today: `apps/web/postcss.config.js` wires
`@tailwindcss/postcss`, `apps/web/app/globals.css` opens with `@import "tailwindcss"` and a `@config` line for
the legacy JS theme, `braces` is absent from both npm locks, and `docs/audit/npm-advisory-exceptions.json`
carries an empty `advisories` list. And this project's product is auditable statistical output, so a
statsmodels bump that could move a p-value is not "clearing a queue". "Handle the dependency queue" ends where
the risk class changes, and saying so is part of handling it.

Corroboration that #107 was worth landing: five of those eight npm PRs touch only the root
`package-lock.json`, never the member lock that `npm --prefix apps/web ci` reads. Before #107 that half-PR shape
was caught late, at the install step, with a message about lockfile satisfaction. Now the dedicated member-lock
guard names the field and both values at the gate -- the failure mode it was written for, observed again the same
day it merged.

## 280. The Render demo is current, and four credential-free answers are what said so

The owner ran **Manual Deploy → Deploy latest commit code** on the service whose External URL reads
`https://data-science-agent-api-h43i.onrender.com` on 2026-10-24, which closes #44 -- the item that had been
carrying two different weights in this ledger: cosmetic while the fixes were only in the repository, load-bearing
from the day `run_python` was shown to be unbounded, because until that deploy the public surface still listed the
exec pair to any anonymous caller.

What changed for a visitor, each half measured rather than read off the dashboard:

- `tools/list` for an unauthenticated caller now publishes the HTTP list rather than the whole registry, and
  `inputSchema` is present on every entry (the pre-fix image published `input_schema`, so a spec-conformant
  client saw tools that looked argument-less).
- A `tools/call` for `run_python` or `run_sql` answers a JSON-RPC `error` with `code: -32000` naming `dsa mcp`;
  the REST shape answers `isError` with the same sentence and a `hint`. Neither reaches the dispatcher.
- `GET /mcp/tools` returns a `count` equal to the length of the list it returned -- the boundary that used to
  count the registry and publish a shorter list.
- `/mcp-app/` carries a per-document `script-src 'sha256-…'` instead of the API-wide `default-src 'none'`, so
  the page the browser used to render as a dead picture runs (§254).
- The route census still agrees (`hosted 25 / local 25`, no difference either way), as it did on 2026-10-21 and
  2026-10-22 when the deployment *was* behind. That is §281's subject.

`/version` reports `4.6.0` on both the old and the new image, so it is not a currency signal, and the web half
needed no deploy at all: Vercel builds `main` on push, and the cold-start copy loop names the chunk that carries
it. The remaining `/mcp` exposure is the one §265 describes and §277 leaves open -- `profile_dataset`'s read and
its path-existence oracle -- which a deploy does not touch.

## 281. The report-currency probe could not have said what this ledger read from it

`docs/hosted-demo.md` told the reader to fetch a published run's HTML report and search it for
`<strong>[a-z]+_[a-z_]+</strong>`, treating a hit as proof that the running container predated the localization
that names validation checks in words a reviewer knows. On 2026-10-21 and again on 2026-10-22 it hit, and both
entries recorded "the deployed container predates that change". Verifying the redeploy is what showed the
instrument, not the deployment, was the problem: the pattern matches the **Tool Calls** section, which names each
tool by its wire identifier on every build, current included. Five hits, all five from that section, and on this
build the section the instruction was about printed its checks as `Evidence coverage` and `Causal language`.

Two properties made the reading worthless, and both are now pinned by
`tests/contract/test_report_currency_probe.py`:

- **The value it demanded was unreachable.** A correct, localized report still matches, so the doc's
  "run it again; when it prints `False`, the artifact matches the repository" could never be satisfied. A probe
  with one reachable outcome is not a test of anything, and this one was being used to decide whether to spend a
  deploy.
- **Its output was not attributable.** `True` is what the Tool Calls section alone produces on a current build, so
  it cannot distinguish that from the pre-localization shape it was written to catch; whether the 2026-10-21 and
  2026-10-22 containers actually carried raw validation keys is not recoverable from the record either way. The two
  entries stand as measurements of the grep, and the redeploy's currency is now decided by the four answers in §280
  instead.

The fix is a different *section*, not a different word list: the exporter writes validation last, so the probe
reads everything after the final `<h2>`. Position rather than heading text is what lets the same one-liner answer
the question on an English report and a Chinese one (`Validation` / `校验`), and the test asserts that positional
precondition directly, so a future edit that appends a section behind validation reddens the test instead of
quieting the probe. Both directions are planted: the scoped probe returns `[]` on the current rendering in either
language, catches `<strong>evidence_coverage</strong>` when it is put back, and the unscoped pattern is asserted
still to match -- outside the validation section only.

The general form, for the next time a document prescribes a grep: ask what the command prints when the thing it
warns about is *absent*. If that answer is the same as when it is present, the document is not measuring, and any
conclusion already drawn from it -- including this ledger's two dated entries, which now read as instrument
readings rather than deployment ones -- is about the grep.

## 282. The bundle probe printed silence, and the phrase it searched for had no owner

§281 was about one document's grep; the same file carried a second instrument with the same shape, found by
reading it instead of running it. The check for *which web bundle the demo serves* greps each deployed chunk for
a phrase from the cold-start copy and echoed a chunk name only on a match. Two holes:

- **No answer on the negative branch.** A reworded sentence and a stale deployment produced identical silence, so
  the reader could not tell "the bundle predates the copy" from "the copy no longer says that". The loop now
  prints its own denominator -- `chunks scanned: 12, carrying the marker: 1`, measured on the live
  `data-science-agent-web.vercel.app` on 2026-10-24 -- and the miss branch states which of the two readings it is.
- **The search string lived only in prose.** `apps/web/lib/locale.ts` owns that sentence, and nothing connected
  the two. The marker is now read out of the document by `tests/contract/test_hosted_demo_bundle_probe.py` and
  required to be live in the locale file, so rewording the copy without telling the probe is a failing test
  rather than a permanently blinded check.

A third defect was in the shell, not the claim: the loop was
`curl ... | grep -o ... | while read -r s`, and a pipeline's `while` body runs in a subshell, so any running
total it kept could not reach the `echo` after `done`. The rewrite iterates with `for s in $(...)` in the shell
that prints. The test asserts both the absence of the pipe-fed `while` and the presence of the in-shell loop, and
it counts the candidate blocks rather than taking the first -- restoring the old block shape made its own
census assertion fail, which is what keeps the three checks from passing on a file that no longer contains the
probe they describe.

Falsified from both sides: rewording `two minutes` to `ninety seconds` in the locale file reddens the marker test
alone, and restoring the old silent loop reddens all three. Both files were restored and re-hashed inside the same
command, and the suite is green on the restored tree.

Also here, because it is the same rot: `tests/contract/test_web_fetch_outcome_vocabulary.py` cited
`docs/hosted-demo.md:175` for a promise this round's edits moved to line 481. A line number in a docstring is a
citation that cannot be checked by anything, so the pointer now names the section (*Troubleshooting the browser
demo*) instead.

## 283. A header that is present and wrong looked like a clean check, in two places in one document

§282's family, found by taking its question to the next block in the same file: *what does this command print
when the thing it warns about is absent?* The MCP App page probe grepped the response headers for
`^content-security-policy` and printed the line when present. Three facts shared one output -- the per-document
policy the fix ships, the API-wide `default-src 'none'` that makes the page's own script refuse to run, and no
header at all because the request never reached the service. The middle one is the defect the section documents,
and it was indistinguishable from success except by reading the header's text while the prose told the reader to
look for a line.

Rewritten as a three-branch probe that names each outcome, and run against the live host: the deployed page prints
`per-document policy: the page may run the script block it actually shipped`, and a host that answers without the
header prints the absence branch, so both directions are exercised on real traffic rather than asserted. The same
grep existed a second time in the "four answers" block, which is what two copies of an instrument do to each other
over time, so the copy now carries the same branches.

`tests/contract/test_hosted_demo_bundle_probe.py` grew two guards. It enumerates the document's CSP blocks rather
than taking one of them, requires each to hold all three branches, and reads the discriminator out of the document
to demand that `document_security_headers()` still emits it for a script-bearing document -- the string is owned
by the producer, not by the prose. Falsified both ways: pointing the probe at a digest prefix the producer never
emits reddens the discriminator guard, and restoring the old silent one-liner in the copied block reddens the
branch test too. Both mutations restored and re-hashed in the same command.

The same reading also corrected a claim in that block's prose: it told the reader the version check "has to name
the tag that was just built, not the one before it". `/version` answered `4.6.0` on the stale image and on the one
that replaced it on 2026-10-24, because no release has been cut since. The route says which wheel is installed and
nothing about whether the deployment is current, which is the one thing a reader was most likely to want from it.
